memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Speak to the Israelites and say to them: 'When anyone among you brings an offering to the LORD, bring as your offering an animal from either the herd or the flock.'" - Lev 1:2 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
"When anyone among you." Not only the priests. Not only the leaders. Not only the wealthy. The door of worship in Israel was open to the ordinary person, and that mattered deeply in a world where religion often belonged to a professional class.

The word translated "offering" is qorban — literally, something brought near. Worship here is not a mood or a feeling. It is bringing something and placing it in God's hands. The Israelite could not come empty-handed, because sin had made a gap, and something had to stand in that gap.

There is a costly honesty in this. The animal came from the worshipper's own herd or flock — his livelihood, his security, his savings. God did not ask for a token from the leftovers. He asked for something that would be missed.

We do not bring animals today, because Christ has been brought near for us once and for all (Heb 10:10). But the pattern of worship has not changed. God still invites anyone — you, whatever your background, whatever your past — and He still asks for what is genuinely yours. Paul puts it plainly: offer your bodies as a living sacrifice (Rom 12:1). The altar has moved from the courtyard to your daily life.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do I bring God what costs me something, or only what I can easily spare?
2. Have I ever felt too ordinary to approach God in worship?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, thank You that Your invitation reaches even me. Teach me to bring You not my leftovers but my life, in response to the Son who gave His all. Amen.
